newsitem.title: UK: UK trade group warns against tax/interest rate cut.
newsitem.headline: UK trade group warns against tax/interest rate cut.

text.p: The British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) urged Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to avoid "inflationary tax cuts" in the November 26 budget and said interest rates should be left on hold.

In its budget submission, it said the government should not consider cuts in personal taxes while the public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) remains so high and demands on public spending are increasing.
"Furthermore, tax cuts at this point could have inflationary consequences," the BCC said.

It said Clarke should reduce the administrative burden on business by cutting red tape and refraining from introducing new indirect taxes, while encouraging re-investment by business through appropriate tax measures.

"Above all, careful management of the economy must not be driven off course by political expediency in an election year," BCC President David Richardson said in a statement. "The needs of British business should at all times be put before short-term political gain."
On monetary policy, the BCC said interest rates should be left on hold and cuts only be made if likely to be sustainable.
"To reduce interest rates further at present, stimulating what is already improving demand, is a risk which could backfire and stoke inflation," it said.
However, raising interest rates at this stage would risk ending the benefits of economic recovery which small firms were only just beginning to feel.

"We cannot see the evidence for taking either risk at present and believe that rates should remain as they are. In the more medium term, interest rates may indeed have to rise. This will be done with our full support where we think the risks of inflation are greater."
The organisation said its members in more than 196,000 businesses regarded the provision of a stable macro-economic environment as the number one priority for government policy.
Other points from the BCC budget submission included:
- the pay-as-you-earn income tax system and national insurance contributions should be fully integrated to reduce bureaucracy and save money;
- tax on benefits in kind should be reviewed;
- no further complexities should be added to the "already burdensome" system of self-assessment for tax;
- the date of the budget should be moved away from the busiest time of the year for retailers as this places too much of a burden on them;
- the government should continue to curb public expenditure but not to the detriment of essential transport and education projects.
